summary: This program stores a library as a list of Book objects instead of plain title strings, then prints the books, counts them, fetches the first one, and shows that a List happily accepts a duplicate entry.

lines.text: List is the interface that describes an ordered, growable sequence; declaring variables with the interface keeps the code free to switch implementations later.
The type parameter is now Book rather than String, so every element carries a title, an author, and a genre together instead of just one piece of text.

lines.code: books.add(new Book("The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes", "Arthur Conan Doyle", "Mystery"));
lines.text: Each add call builds a fresh Book from three constructor arguments and appends it to the end of the list.
The enhanced for loop walks the list from front to back, handing each element to the loop variable in turn.
Printing an object calls its toString method automatically, which is why Book needs a sensible toString to produce readable output.
size() reports how many elements the list currently holds, and \n inserts a blank line before the label.
A List keeps its elements in insertion order and indexes them from zero, so get(0) returns the first book added.
This is a second, separate Book object with identical field values; a List never checks for duplicates, so it is stored alongside the original.

lines.code: System.out.println("Total number of books after adding duplicate: " + books.size());
lines.text: The count rises to four, demonstrating that duplicates are allowed in a List and motivating the Set collection later in the chapter.
